questions.explain: The chapter states RDS for SQL Server has no cross-region read replica, so DR on AWS is assembled from backup-based mechanisms: snapshot copy, native backups to S3 with CRR, or distributed AGs on EC2.
options: Cross-region read replicas
Backup-based mechanisms like cross-region snapshot copy and native backups to S3 with CRR
Azure failover groups
Hyperscale named replicas
questions.q: RDS for SQL Server has no cross-region read replica. What DR mechanisms does the chapter recommend on AWS?

questions.explain: Azure auto-failover groups bundle databases into a primary and secondary region with a single listener endpoint, automatic failover policy with a configurable grace period; RPO is seconds and RTO is the grace period plus promotion time.
options: Read replicas with manual DNS
Auto-failover groups with a single listener endpoint, configurable grace period, and seconds-level RPO
Log shipping via Azure Automation
Export/import pipelines
questions.q: What is Azure's most integrated cross-region DR mechanism for SQL Database and Managed Instance?

questions.explain: Native backup files in S3 with cross-region replication give RPO equal to log backup frequency (15 minutes typical) — the finest RPO available for SQL Server DR on AWS without a running secondary.
options: Hours, like snapshot copy
Days, based on S3 lifecycle policies
Minutes — RPO equals the log backup frequency
Zero, because S3 replication is synchronous
questions.q: What RPO does the chapter attribute to native backups to S3 with cross-region replication?

questions.explain: Replication copies corruption and ransomware to every replica — that's its job. Logical disaster must be defended with backups: immutable backups (S3 Object Lock), geo-restore, and LTR copies.
options: Async replication lag is zero
Replication cannot copy ransomware
Replication is its job — it copies corruption faithfully, so logical disaster needs backups
Failover groups block logical disasters automatically
questions.q: Why does the chapter say replication cannot save you from a logical disaster (mass deletion or ransomware)?

questions.explain: The chapter recommends setting the database hostname DNS TTL low (60 seconds) permanently — not just during drills — so failover propagation isn't delayed.
options: Set the TTL to 24 hours for stability
Disable DNS caching entirely
Set the database hostname TTL low (60 seconds) permanently
Use a new hostname after every drill
questions.q: For DNS-based client redirection in DR, what DNS TTL practice does the chapter recommend?
